Operator:
Good morning, and welcome to the Stratosphere Industries Third Quarter Earnings Conference Call. All participants will be in listen-only mode. After today's presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. As a reminder, ladies and gentlemen, this conference is being recorded. I would now like to turn the conference over to Emily Carter, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Emily Carter:
Thank you, Operator, and good morning, everyone. Welcome to Stratosphere Industries' Third Quarter Fiscal 2024 Earnings Conference Call. Joining me today are Alex Rivera, Chief Executive Officer; Jordan Hayes, Chief Financial Officer; Taylor Brooks, Chief Operating Officer; and Riley Patel, Chief Technology Officer.

Before we begin, I'd like to remind you that this call contains forward-looking statements within the meaning of the safe harbor provisions of the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995. Please refer to our SEC filings, including our most recent Form 10-K and 10-Q, for a complete discussion of risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially from those expressed or implied in these statements.

Alex Rivera:
Thank you, Emily, and good morning, everyone. Stratosphere Industries delivered a solid performance in the third quarter of fiscal 2024, demonstrating the resilience of our business model and the strength of our diversified portfolio across defense, commercial aviation, and space systems. Our priorities remain focused on executing our strategy, driving operational excellence, and delivering long-term value to our shareholders. Today, we will cover key areas including our overall performance highlights, revenue drivers and headwinds, aftermarket performance drivers, book-to-bill ratio, and the defense budget outlook with its impact on our business.

We are particularly excited about the recent advancements in our ARROW-6 hypersonic glide vehicle program and its potential to accelerate our future growth through leadership in high-speed strike capabilities. We are seeing strong demand for our defense systems, including fixed-wing aircraft and next-gen C4ISR platforms, and our commercial aerospace business is recovering steadily with robust aftermarket support.

With that, I'll turn it over to Jordan to provide more details on our financial results and these strategic aspects.

Jordan Hayes:
Thank you, Alex, and good morning, everyone. Let's turn to the financials for the third quarter ended September 30, 2024. We reported revenue of $8.7 billion, representing a 14 percent increase year-over-year and 5 percent sequentially. This marks our 11th consecutive quarter of double-digit top-line growth, driven by defense sustainment, commercial ramps, and space opportunities. Adjusted earnings per share came in at $2.68, surpassing our guidance midpoint by $0.13 and up 22 percent from last year, thanks to operational leverage and pricing discipline despite inflation.

We continue to maintain a strong balance sheet with $6.2 billion in cash and equivalents. Our funded backlog stands at a record $128 billion, up 8 percent quarter-over-quarter. Free cash flow generation was exceptional at $1.2 billion, or 14 percent of revenue, which allowed us to execute $750 million in share repurchases and announce a 12 percent dividend increase this morning. Segment operating margins expanded across the board: defense at 13.2 percent, commercial aviation at 9.8 percent, and space and advanced systems at 11.5 percent, reflecting our cost-out initiatives and supply chain resilience.

Gross margin was 22.1 percent, operating income reached $1.8 billion, and free cash flow hit that $1.2 billion mark. Our full-year guidance has been raised: FY24 revenue now at $34.5 to $35.0 billion, up from prior $34 to $34.8 billion; EPS at $10.60 to $10.80, up from $10.40 to $10.70. For Q4, we expect revenue of $8.9 to $9.1 billion and EPS of $2.85 to $2.95. We are actively managing costs, investing in growth, and returning capital through dividends and buybacks.

Let me break down our overall company performance highlights and key takeaways. Defense accounted for 62 percent of revenues at $5.4 billion, up 16 percent year-over-year. This was driven by accelerated deliveries on the F-47 Lightning II program, where we achieved 95 percent yield on wing assemblies ahead of schedule, contributing $1.2 billion. Hypersonic initiatives gained traction with our HAWC-derived booster securing a $2.8 billion indefinite delivery indefinite quantity contract from DARPA and the Air Force, positioning us strongly in the Glide Breaker competition.

Sustainment and services grew 20 percent to $2.1 billion, supported by C-17 Globemaster IV depot overhauls for the U.S. Air Force and rising foreign military sales demand from NATO allies amid Ukraine tensions. U.S. DoD funding remains our foundation at 55 percent of segment sales, but international exposure reached 28 percent, up from 24 percent last year, with growth in the Middle East from Saudi MQ-9 Reaper upgrades and in the Indo-Pacific from Australian Loyal Wingman integrations. Margins expanded 110 basis points to 13.2 percent on improved labor utilization and fixed-price wins achieving 98 percent award fees.

Commercial aviation contributed 28 percent of revenues at $2.4 billion, up 12 percent year-over-year as OEM recovery picks up. Boeing 737 MAX and 787 wing spar production increased to 45 ships per month, securing 18 percent share in composites, while Airbus A320neo fuselage sections benefited from our new Greenville automation line, cutting touch labor by 35 percent. Aftermarket MRO revenues jumped 25 percent to $850 million, powered by engine overhauls and our AI-driven ForgePredict platform, which reduced unscheduled maintenance by 22 percent for Delta and United fleets.

Titanium supply constraints posed challenges, similar to Boeing's 737 issues, but dual-sourcing from VSMPO-AVISMA and U.S. alternatives limited impact to under 2 percent of output. Margins rose to 9.8 percent thanks to pass-through clauses covering 85 percent of inflation, though we anticipate some Q4 pressure from labor escalations.

Space and advanced systems, at 10 percent of revenues or $900 million, grew 22 percent year-over-year, outperforming the market. We completed the first orbital test of our Nova-6 reusable upper stage for NASA's Artemis SLS Block 2, earning a $1.5 billion follow-on, and scaled laser comms terminals for proliferated LEO constellations hardened for the DoD's Blackjack program. We booked $4.2 billion in new awards, including a hypersonic missile defense sensor suite with the Missile Defense Agency.

U.S. Space Force pursuits for NSSL Phase 3 are ramping, with Europe contributing via ESA's Ariane 6. Margins reached 11.5 percent through vertical integration of gallium nitride RF components, reducing subcontractor reliance by 40 percent.

Company-wide, we're investing $450 million in FY24 capex, with 80 percent toward digital transformation. Our ForgeTwin digital twin ecosystem now spans 70 percent of programs, speeding design iterations by 15 percent and improving yields by 12 percent on assemblies like directed energy prototypes. Sustainability advanced with 25 percent sustainable aviation fuel certification on test fleets, supporting FAA mandates and net-zero goals.

Supply chain metrics strengthened: inventory days on hand fell to 145 from 162, with 92 percent on-time delivery versus 85 percent last year. Geopolitical events like Ukraine, Taiwan Straits, and Red Sea issues heightened demand for ISR and missile defense, while U.S. supplementals added $3.1 billion to our pipeline.

Strategically, we emphasize program stability, innovation adjacency, and shareholder returns. Defense anchors low double-digit growth through the decade on the FY25 NDAA. Commercial OEM projects 18 to 20 percent growth in FY25 as Boeing stabilizes. Space targets 25 percent plus CAGR to $5 billion by FY27 via partnerships. Risks include 4.2 percent inflation on inputs, labor shortages—we hired up 15 percent with 98 percent retention—and potential sequestration, but 42 percent backlog coverage and liquidity buffer us.

Key takeaways: execution excellence with beat-and-raise results validating predictable growth; balanced portfolio diversifying risks; geopolitical moat for visibility; innovation edge in digital twins, hypersonics, and SAF; and the raised guidance. Total shareholder return up 28 percent YTD versus the S&P A&D index's 15 percent.

Turning to an analysis of our revenue drivers and headwinds this quarter. Revenues totaled $8.7 billion, up 14 percent year-over-year and 8 percent sequentially, supported by 1.3x book-to-bill and $145 billion backlog up 22 percent year-over-year. Defense systems at 52 percent or $4.5 billion grew 21 percent, fueled by the F-47 Lightning II as Tier 1 supplier for mission systems and composites, with 25 percent ramp from Lot 15-17 LRIP deliveries at $1.2 billion. FRP shift in FY25 with 156 aircraft funded promises mid-teens growth, plus international to Israel and Poland at $450 million up 30 percent.

Hypersonics and missile defense added $850 million up 40 percent via HAWC derivatives and Glide Phase Interceptor for MDA, leveraging scramjet tech. Unmanned systems like Loyal Wingman generated $600 million from USAF CCA initiatives, with YTD bookings over $2 billion at 1.5x book-to-bill. North America at 75 percent, EMEA up 35 percent on NATO F-47 sustainment, APAC 12 percent via AUKUS.

Commercial aviation at 32 percent or $2.8 billion up 12 percent, with MRO and aftermarket at 60 percent or $1.7 billion up 18 percent from high utilization on 737NG and A320ceo fleets. Wheel-and-brake and nacelle MRO for PW1100G spiked 22 percent as airlines defer new buys. OEM narrowbody at $1.1 billion for 737 MAX and A321neo composites, 95 percent take rates despite Boeing slips; widebody $300 million.

Space at 16 percent or $1.4 billion up 5 percent, $750 million from NRO/SDA satellites, $400 million laser comms for LEO DoD apps. Enablers include additive manufacturing cutting titanium lead times 30 percent for 98 percent delivery, SAF certification for upgrades.

Headwinds trimmed upside by 300 basis points. Supply chain: titanium inflation 20-25 percent post-sanctions, 6-9 month delays, PW1000G groundings, Boeing shortages deferred $400 million—mitigated by Japan/U.S. sourcing for Q4 normalization. Labor/inflation: 15 percent machinist wages, 12 percent aluminum/carbon fiber, commercial RPK growth 4.5 percent versus pre-COVID 6 percent delayed $250 million APAC. Geopolitics: Middle East boosts but FMS delays; Saudi Vision offsets with $1.5 billion THAAD; FAA/EASA backlogs slip 3-6 months; China MAX curbs shave 5 percent commercial.

Outlook: FY24 $34-36 billion midpoint up 13 percent, Defense 20 percent plus, MRO offsets OEM. Margins to 12.5 percent via LEAN, hypersonics share to 25 percent. FY25 bids $2 billion NGAD/lunar. Balance sheet enables M&A.

Now, on drivers of our aftermarket performance, which delivered $2.8 billion, up 18 percent year-over-year and 42 percent of segment sales. This is nine straight quarters of double-digit growth, with EBITDA margins up 320 basis points to 32.5 percent from high-value MRO and digital services mix.

Fleet utilization rebounded sharply to 87 percent globally per IATA from 58 percent lows, driving 22 percent higher block hours on our 25,000 commercial engines and 15,000 avionics. Narrowbodies at 92 percent utilization for A320neo/737 MAX from capacity constraints and leisure travel; widebodies 81 percent stabilizing. Defense at 95 percent plus for F-47 and F/A-18, F135 sustainment $450 million up 25 percent on 1.2 million hours. Each 1 percent block hour rise lifts LLPs/hot-sections 2.5 percent; Q3 added $180 million.

Maintenance cycles elongated strategically: GAD-LEAP on-wing to 28,000 cycles up 12 percent via CMCs/coatings, ASP to $4.2 million with HOVs 65 percent. Airframe C-checks to 24 months via Touchless Heavy Maintenance robotics, San Antonio throughput 120 aircraft. F-47 PDM up 20 percent via propulsion health management averting $120 million downtime. Book-to-bill 1.25x, $3.5 billion new contracts including $1.2 billion 10-year Delta A320neo.

Tech like Fleet Diagnostics Platform on 85 percent base predicts 95 percent accurately, cutting unscheduled by 25 percent, PHM extends 1,500 hours, Q3 $250 million at 40 percent margins. Additive for PMA CFM56 spares 30 percent in-house at 40 percent less cost.

Regions: APAC 28 percent growth to $950 million from C919 avionics, IndiGo 95 percent utilization, 1,200 narrowbodies by 2028. EMEA 16 percent Ryanair/BAE Eurofighter, NATO 2.1 percent GDP. North America 12 percent offset by DoD $10 billion F-47. LATAM 65 percent hedged by Embraer.

Aftermarket TAM $120 billion, our 28 percent share up from 24 percent via exclusivity on Boom Overture, GE/HAL AMCA. Risks titanium up 15 percent, but 98 percent delivery. Q4 $2.9-$3.0 billion, full-year 17-19 percent growth, 33 percent margins—predictable cash, 10x ROIC.

Regarding our book-to-bill ratio, overall we achieved 1.22x in the quarter, up from 1.15x last year and 1.18x prior quarter—eighth straight above 1.0x. Orders $24.8 billion versus $20.3 billion revenue grew backlog to $158 billion, up 7 percent year-over-year and 3 percent sequentially.

This reflects DoD FYDP emphasis on China/Russia competition. Awards: $4.2 billion F-47 Lot 16 LRIP, $1.8 billion hypersonic boost-glide for Army LRHW to TRL 7. U.S. 72 percent at $17.9 billion (1.25x), international $6.9 billion (1.16x) via FMS Middle East THAAD, Europe Patriot/JASSM Ukraine aid, APAC 1.30x P-8 variant $900 million.

Aeronautics 1.12x: $9.1 billion orders on $8.1 billion revenue; defense fixed-wing $2.5 billion B-21 ECP, F-47 sustainment $1.1 billion TR-3 Block 4. Commercial 0.98x from Boeing/Airbus delays, offset $1.2 billion 787 SAF wing. Backlog $52 billion, 40 percent defense.

Missiles & fire control 1.35x: $7.2 billion on $5.3 billion, backlog $48 billion up 12 percent. $2.1 billion hypersonics ARRW HAWC follow-on, $1.4 billion HIMARS Ukraine. U.S. 55 percent $28 billion missile budget, Europe 30 percent NATO munitions, Indo-Pacific 15 percent. $250 million digital twins for hypersonic tests, 20 percent FRIP cost-out.

Rotary & mission systems 1.18x: $5.6 billion on $4.7 billion, backlog $35 billion up 6 percent. MH-60R Australia $800 million, MQ-25 IOC; commercial H175 Asia 1.05x. C4ISR $1.0 billion JADC2.

Space systems 1.28x: $2.9 billion on $2.2 billion, backlog $23 billion up 11 percent. NASA Artemis HLS $700 million, NSSL Phase 3 Vulcan $1.1 billion, LEO laser $400 million. U.S. Space Force 68 percent, EUSPA Galileo. $150 million reusable launch for 30 percent cost cut vs. Starship.

75 percent backlog funded, 60 percent international. AI supply analytics counters inflation/labor. 18-20 percent 2025 growth assuming no CRs. Risks OEM delays, rare earths, but 45 percent recurring sustainment.

Finally, on the defense budget outlook and its impact on Stratosphere Industries. Globally, SIPRI projects $2.44 trillion in 2024 defense spending, up 6.8 percent year-over-year—the sharpest in a decade—with 7 to 9 percent CAGR through FY28, driven by China/Russia threats demanding hypersonics like ARROW-6 Mach 8 in DT&E and Loyal Wingman CCA.

U.S. core: FY25 request $886 billion DoD base up 4.1 percent from $851 billion, plus $112 billion OCO for Ukraine/Israel/Indo-Pacific. NDAA House adds $25 billion for NGAD, B-21, hypersonics. Procurement/RDT&E $323 billion up 7.2 percent, aircraft $72 billion up 9 percent, missiles $41 billion up 12 percent.

For us, F-47 LRIP Lot 18 $14.2 billion total, our 28 percent or $4.0 billion on 42 percent OEM share; FRP FY26 block buys 1,200+ units at $98 million flyaway. Book-to-bill 1.4x, backlog $112 billion up 15 percent YoY, 4.2 years visibility at $28.5 billion FY24 midpoint.

Europe breakout: NATO 23/32 at 2 percent GDP, €325 billion up 12 percent. Germany €100 billion Zeus PAC-3 MSE €2.1 billion Q3; Poland Wisla $1.8 billion hypersonics. Europe FY25 revenue 18 percent up from 12 percent FY22, margins 14.5 percent fixed-price.

Asia-Pacific: Australia $368 billion 72 F-47s $8.5 billion potential; Japan GCAP CCA $2.3 billion MoU; India MRFA Rafale 114 platforms 25 percent workshare. Regional 22 percent backlog, 9 percent growth.

Middle East/Gulf 7 percent: Saudi $80 billion Vision $27 billion airpower, THOR directed-energy $450 million; Israel Iron Dome $1.2 billion annual.

Quality trends: hypersonics $3.2 billion FY25, CCA Lot 1 $1.1 billion, digital engineering cut F-47 costs 22 percent. FY25 R&D $1.8 billion or 6.3 percent sales for AI/ML logistics, quantum comms.

FY25 guidance: revenue $30.2-$31.1 billion up 8-10 percent, margins 13.8-14.3 percent up 110 bps, FCF $3.5-$4.0 billion. 85 percent backlog funded, 65 percent fixed-price up from 52 percent FY21. Risks sequestration delaying $5-7 billion, buffered by $18 billion international, $45 billion classified.

Multi-year budgets resume peak-trough-peak; our 28 percent tactical aircraft share, 35 percent hypersonics for 12-15 percent EPS CAGR FY28. We're shaping the cycle via tech.

That wraps our prepared remarks on these critical areas.

Taylor Brooks:
Thank you, Jordan. Operationally, we've made significant strides in supply chain management, boosting production rates on key programs like the F-47 and hypersonics. Investments in automation and digital technologies, including our ForgeTwin platform across 70 percent of operations, have enhanced efficiency, cut costs by 12 to 15 percent on complex assemblies, and improved on-time delivery to 92 percent. Inventory optimization reduced days on hand to 145, while dual-sourcing and additive manufacturing have de-risked titanium and rare earth dependencies. Our teams achieved 98 percent retention amid hiring growth, supporting ramps in MRO hubs and LRIP lots.

Riley Patel:
To add a technology note, our focus on AI-driven predictive maintenance, digital twins, and hypersonic testing facilities positions us ahead in NGAD, Artemis, and JADC2 integrations.

Operator:
Thank you. We will now begin the question and answer session. Our first question comes from Mike Thompson with Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.

Mike Thompson:
Good morning. Can you provide more color on the defense budget outlook and its specific impact on your backlog conversion?

Alex Rivera:
Certainly, Mike. As Jordan outlined, the FY25 request and NDAA trajectory provide strong tailwinds, with our F-47 Lot 18 capture and international like Germany's Zeus driving the 1.4x book-to-bill and $112 billion backlog. Over 85 percent funded ensures steady conversion, even with potential CR delays buffered by diversified offsets.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Laura Chen with JPMorgan. Please go ahead.

Laura Chen:
Hi, thanks. I'm curious about the book-to-bill trends by segment and any shifts in international mix?

Jordan Hayes:
Laura, great question. Overall 1.22x with missiles at 1.35x leading on hypersonics and HIMARS, aeronautics stabilizing at 1.12x despite commercial OEM pressures, and space at 1.28x from NSSL and Artemis. International strengthened to over 28 percent of bookings, particularly EMEA and APAC, enhancing margin resilience with fixed-price exports.

Operator:
Our next question comes from David Kim with Morgan Stanley. Please go ahead.

David Kim:
Regarding the drivers of aftermarket performance, how sustainable is the utilization rebound and margin expansion?

Taylor Brooks:
David, fleet utilization at 87 percent commercial and 95 percent defense is sustainable with ongoing travel demand and geopolitical ops. Extended cycles via CMCs and PHM boost shop visit values, while FDP tech shifts to 40 percent margin digital services. We're guiding 17-19 percent full-year growth, crown jewel for cash flow.

Alex Rivera:
Thank you for your questions. In closing, I'm confident in our ability to navigate the current environment and deliver long-term value to our shareholders. We remain focused on our strategic priorities, operational excellence, and innovation leadership in aerospace and defense.

Emily Carter:
Thank you for joining us today. This concludes our Third Quarter Fiscal 2024 Earnings Conference Call. A replay and transcript will be available on our investor relations website.

Operator:
This concludes today's conference call. Thank you for participating. You may now disconnect.
